title: Why Technology Hasn’t Boosted Learning—And How It Could
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Reviewing Daisy Christodoulou's Teachers vs. Tech?, Wexler argues that billions spent on classroom technology have produced little because its use rests on mistaken beliefs about learning. Ed tech mostly replicates ineffective approaches, whereas an understanding of learning science lets it help students move chunked content into long-term memory through adaptive retrieval practice. She walks through why personalization, flipped classrooms, device distraction and search skills as a substitute for knowledge fall short, citing the Tree Octopus hoax experiment. She adds a US-specific misuse in reading comprehension skills software and recounts misinformation in an education school technology class. She closes with Christodoulou's optimism that technology can help if bad ideas are disrupted first.
points: Ed tech underdelivers because it is built on the belief that facts and long-term memory do not matter.
Used well, technology can chunk content and adapt retrieval practice, as in math and language learning apps.
Personalization by learning styles or student choice, and flipped classrooms, fail because novices cannot direct their own learning.
Devices in class invite distraction, and no one is good at multi-tasking.
Search skills cannot replace knowledge, as seven graders judged a hoax tree octopus site credible for lack of background.
quotes: Ed tech is mostly just replicating existing ineffectual approaches to teaching, and sometimes making them worse.
That’s important, because the evidence shows that the more information you have in long-term memory, the more cognitive capacity you have for comprehension, analysis, and additional learning.
To think critically about a topic, you need to have information about it; the more information you have, the better you can analyze it.
And students who aren’t already competent in a field are ill-equipped to direct their own learning.
Of the 25 students, 24 found the website “very credible.” They would have been in a far better position if they’d had some basic information about octopuses.
But it’s often used for practice in reading comprehension “skills” like “finding the main idea.” That kind of instruction doesn’t work, whether it’s delivered by a computer or a human being.
Before we can harness the power of technology to improve learning, we have to first understand how learning works—and that means reversing mistaken assumptions that have been entrenched for decades.
